paragraphs.text: Lately the great and God-befitting manifestation of the Savior set a rich table before us. It mixed an overflowing bowl of divine philosophy and made the whole people drunk, or rather, so to speak, the whole world. For "They shall be drunk," says the prophet, "with the richness of your house, and you will give them to drink from the torrent of your delight." When the divine Scripture speaks of drunkenness, it does not mean wine that intoxicates but a word that makes wise. The fruit of repentance followed upon the Savior's coming. It was fitting that the fruits of repentance should follow the Savior's shining forth. That is why yesterday our sermon took up this subject. It fell far short of the worth of the matter before us, yet it did not hold back what strength it had. It spoke of repentance, which is the medicine of salvation. It proclaimed a physician of souls and bodies, who heals not by applying medicines but by a nod of his love for humankind. But the Gospel reading slipped past our minds while we were distracted this way and that. So today it is necessary to go through it briefly with you, and so bring the discourse to a close.

The Savior taught piety by word, and he set before the faithful what was good for them by parables, riddles and various ways of teaching. He told a parable that holds a powerful image of repentance. "A certain man," he says, "had two sons." The younger of them came and asked his father to divide the property between them. He got what he asked for, and after he had received his father's property he disposed of it badly. The story you know. But it is worth bringing out its deeper meaning here. For even if the many may understand it in different ways, the truth makes itself clear to those who are well disposed.

What, then, does the fount of wisdom set forth here? The first order, that of the righteous, and the second order, that of those made righteous through repentance. The first have honored righteousness from the beginning; the second are brought back to righteousness by repentance. "A certain man had two sons." Choice has separated the ungodly from the godly, yet truth knows them all as one creature of the Creator, and all are sons of God, even if by their evil mind they cut themselves off from their own dignity. Hence, if we depart from piety through evil desires, God does not deny the kinship. Even to the rebellious he speaks with a father's voice: "Return to me, you rebellious sons, and I will return to you." Do you see that even when the sinner's mind has turned away, God does not disdain to call those who have turned away his sons? For he knows the creature he formed as his own, and he does not disown his own kindness.

Why, then, did the younger son misuse what he was given? What lies before us is a riddle. Hear how. From the beginning righteousness existed; it appeared and shone forth. But sin was brought into the world as something younger and recent. That is why the first son is not put in the place of the one who spent badly. For the original creation possessed perfect beauty when the world was new, shining with new grace and new beauty. Moses bears witness to the beauty of creation when he says, "And all things were good," and not simply good, but "very good." So righteousness came first, and the good is most ancient. Sin was younger. It came in upon righteousness and muddied its beauty. So he divided his goods between them equally. Why equally? Because the righteous have nothing more in the present life, since he "makes the sun rise on the righteous and the unrighteous, and sends rain on the good and the evil." But the son who is pictured in the place of the righteous did not want to divide the father's inheritance; he remained under the father's authority. For the righteous man always follows God and draws nothing away into his own control. Do you want to learn that the righteous man wishes to take nothing from God, but keeps in step only with the ordering and providence of that same Father? David cries out from the order of the righteous: "What have I in heaven? And what have I desired from you on earth?" Do you see that the order of the righteous does not want to seize authority over created things for itself? It wants the affairs of the household to rest under the Father's providence. But the younger son took his father's property and went abroad into a far country. It was not separated from home by distance but cut off by his way of life. For the sinner is far from God, brothers, not in place but in manner, as it is said: "Behold, those who remove themselves far from you shall perish." Having received his father's property, he squandered it in riotous living: he defiled with sin the creation he had received. He received the sun to enjoy, and he worshiped the gift as a god. He received springs for his delight, and he thought the gift a god. The Giver was ignored and the gifts were honored, as Paul cries out in distress: "And they served the creature rather than the Creator." The same creation [?], the same paternal property: one son used it well, the other badly. So it is with the one order and the other: one acts well, the other the opposite. The godly man sees the beauty of heaven, and from its beauty he comes to know its Maker: "For I will behold the heavens, the works of your fingers." He saw the beauty and gave thanks to the one who made such beauty. He saw the ordered world and praised the one who set it in order. For the godly man praises creation but worships the Creator. When the godly refuse to worship visible things, they do not insult creation; they render honor to the Master. The believer does not hate the sun just because he does not revere the light as the ungodly do. He sets a limit to the honor he gives it. He both honors and loves visible things as gifts of God. Do you want to see how the godly man looks on beauty and admires it, yet reserves his worship for the Creator? One of the wise says (I mean those wise in piety): "The sun shining in the heights of the Lord, a marvelous vessel, a mighty work, breathing out fiery rays, lighting up the heavens." And what follows at once? "Great is the Lord who made it." He proclaimed the beauty and did not hide the craftsman. But the ungodly man looked wrongly on "the heavens declaring the glory of God," which they declare not in words but by the beauty of creation. Heaven has never burst out with a voice, yet by its splendor it gives a testimony more powerful than a voice. Does heaven declare the glory of God while silent? Certainly it does. Your letters speak while silent; do God's elements not speak, though silent? You have had a taste of piety; from the taste, take hold of the whole of the truth. Now look at the part of the ungodly man, and see how he stumbles over the very things by which the righteous man is made righteous. He sees the moon and worships it; he sees the stars and reveres them; he sees the sea and makes it a god. Those who were in the Babylonian furnace, who went into it, sang hymns to God through his works with their saving and noble confession, saying, "Bless the Lord, all you works of the Lord." It would have been enough to say these words and end the hymn. For God takes his rest not in the length of hymns but in the purpose of those who sing them. By saying "all the works," then, they included everything, and there was no need to add anything. But they were not preaching to themselves. They were singing to God, and through the hymn they were teaching the Chaldeans who stood by. So the hymn had to pass through the whole of creation, so that the deluded Chaldeans might learn what is praised and what things give the praise.

But the discourse has led us into much contemplation, so let us leave that for now and return to our subject. The younger son went abroad into a far country, wasted his property badly and began to be in want. "The rich have become poor and hungry, but those who seek the Lord shall lack no good thing." "For the Lord will not withhold good things from those who walk in innocence." He began to be in want. "And he attached himself to one of the rulers of that country, and the man sent him to feed pigs." See how great was the height of his former nobility, and how great the humiliation of the one who cut himself off from piety! He was given pigs to feed, that is, he was given over to wallowing in pleasures and sins. For what mire is to pigs, sin is to those who wallow in it. That is why the Savior said, alluding to those who live in impurity and wallow in sins as in mire: "Do not give what is holy to dogs, and do not throw your pearls before pigs." He fed pigs.

"And he longed to fill himself with the carob pods that the pigs were eating, and no one gave him any." Pay close attention here. The man who cuts himself off from piety does not even enjoy the pleasures themselves. He is subjected to want and condemned to poverty, so that he does not even have plenty of the evils he chose. For "the fool," it says, "will die in want." So he likens the pleasures of the world to carob pods. The carob pod has a great deal of roughness and little sweetness. So too the bright and desirable things of the world bring much toil and little enjoyment. Our whole life is yoked to more labor than gladness. "For the days of our years, in them are seventy years, and most of them are toil and trouble." In the end, want disciplined him and affliction turned him back. "Your apostasy will discipline you, and your wickedness will reprove you."

"But when he came to himself." "To himself" is well said. For when we sin we are outside ourselves; we are out of our minds; we are carried away outside our own reasoning. But when we make progress in righteousness, we return to ourselves. "When he came to himself," it says. Here pay close attention, and see how true is what was said earlier: physicians prescribe remedies that come from outside and belong to others, but the remedies for our life we have within ourselves. "When he came to himself." He used no remedy from outside. He used his own, the advantages he had by nature; these he used for his salvation. And he says: "How many of my father's hired servants have bread to spare, while I am perishing with hunger?" The divine Scripture calls "sons" those who are wholly devoted to righteousness and piety. It calls "hired servants" those who are not wholly disposed toward him, and who do not set their minds entirely on the things of God in the way they live. They understand the good and love the word, but they have not given their whole mind to him. And to these, who have the longing in full and are wholly devoted to piety [?], God gives a wage in proportion to their purpose. Fittingly, then, the son says: "How many of my father's hired servants have bread to spare, while I am perishing with hunger? I will return to my father." "I will return," in the words of the one who says, "Return, my soul, to your rest."

"And I will say: Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you, and I am no longer worthy to be called your son; make me like one of your hired servants." The words of the one who repents are one thing, and the words of the one who receives his repentance are another. The man who comes from sins to repentance does not imagine the kingdom of heaven. He does not judge himself worthy of eternal life. He has only one prayer: to be rescued from Gehenna. So he expects little, but God bestows on him an abundant wealth of kindness. O, what a wonder! He had only thought of repentance, and at once the father ran ahead of him with his love. He did not wait to hear the words of confession; he forestalled the request, as it is said: "Before you call on me, I will say, Here I am." He saw his son coming from far off and went out to meet him. Do you see how love for humankind outruns repentance? That is why David too, having stripped off the disease of sin with the medicine of repentance, and knowing that God in his love goes out to meet those who approach him, entreats God, saying: "Rise up to meet me, and see" that I come to you sincerely, that I put on repentance in truth. The father received his child, and the son said to the father: "I have sinned; I am no longer worthy to be called your son; make me like one of your hired servants."

Here the father makes no speech to him. He does not answer him, but says to the servants: "Bring out the first robe for him." What does the riddle mean? The penitent prays for many things. He receives no answer in words, but he sees love in action. Here we are taught that our repentance is expressed in words, but God's love in deeds. "Bring out the first robe for him," the one he lost through his transgression. "Give him sandals too." Why? Because the serpent has been made the enemy of sinners, as it is said: "He will watch for your head, and you will watch for his heel." He puts sandals on him for safety, so that the deadly serpent may not come at a bare foot and pour out the venom of sin once more on one who has been freed from sin. If he does not receive the sandals, he cannot "tread on serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy." That is why Paul, guarding against the serpent's bites, proclaimed in the reading just now: "I fear that, as the serpent deceived Eve, so your minds may be corrupted from the simplicity that is in Christ."

But here, like some new drama, that much-discussed question comes up. For many find fault with creation. "Why," one asks, "was the serpent in paradise? Why did the tree bring about such a host of evils? Why did the Creator plant such a plant? Is it not absurd? A human gardener takes pains to drive out contrary seeds and foreign weeds from among his own seed, and to keep his land clean of whatever opposes it. Yet God, after setting up so great and so vast a paradise, made a plant from which the source of evils was to spring." The divine Paul leads us to this line of thought when he says: "I fear that, as the serpent deceived Eve, so your minds may be corrupted from the simplicity that is in Christ." What then, brothers? Let us leave aside the many superfluous points that are examined in detail and come to the heart of the matter. God made all things good, and not simply good but "very good." The addition shows the height of beauty in everything that came to be. So God gives Adam abundance and enjoyment, and the authority both to enjoy paradise and to rule the visible world. "Let us make man in our image and likeness, and let them rule over the fish of the sea, and the birds of heaven, and the wild beasts, and the cattle, and all the earth." Here he gave him authority over paradise; he gave him delight and enjoyment. So Adam was an appointed king, with authority over visible things and the enjoyment of paradise. It was therefore necessary that Adam be given a commandment to train his soul in obedience.

Many say: "Did God not know that Adam would transgress? Why, then, did he give a law to one who was going to transgress?" I beg you, beloved, to join me in the struggle of this laborious argument. For we are making a defense on behalf of what God formed, on behalf of God's handiwork. He made man. He gave him abundance of all things. He commands him to eat of everything. Now if the commandment had been narrow, allowing him to touch a few things and requiring him to abstain from most, the transgression would have had a plausible excuse: the narrowness of his enjoyment would have given his will a pretext to lean the wrong way. But if the abundance was great and what was forbidden was small, why did he not honor his benefactor by obeying? But someone might say that God gave him abundance of many things, yet Adam saw no such beauty in any other tree, since this one was lovely to the sight and good to the taste. So, to remove even this plausible defense, God gave the same beauty he gave that tree to all the others as well. For Moses says: "And God made to spring up also every tree lovely to the sight and good for food." Why, then, was the commandment given? So that Adam might learn that he was under a law and a master. And why did he give this commandment and not another? There was no other training ground for obedience. What should God have said to Adam? "You shall not steal"? Steal whose things? What law should God have laid down? "You shall not murder"? Murder whom? "You shall not commit adultery"? With whose wife? "You shall not covet"? Covet what belongs to whom? The commandment had nothing to work on. The world did not yet exist as it now is, nor the confusion that now fills it. But surely he should have said, "You shall not bring false accusations"? What court was there? Who were the accusers, or who the accused? So he gives him a commandment drawn from the enjoyment set before him: to have abundance of everything, but to abstain from this one tree alone. In this way, while enjoying everything, he would have before him the lordship that forbade the tree. It was not that the tree itself was anything other than good; rather, the transgression was wicked. Consider a parallel. The law of nature wants a virgin to be given away as a bride in lawful marriage. But if a virgin gets ahead of her father's appointed time, or of the season for marriage, and gives herself up to licentiousness, she is liable under the laws to a punishment that cannot be escaped. This is not because she has experienced something different from other virgins, but because she gave herself to sin against the law that pleased her father. She is punished not for the nature of the act but for the manner of the transgression. So too Adam became liable to punishment, not as one who had touched something forbidden in itself, but as one who had taken for himself what the commandment forbade.

Read the records. Why do you quarrel about things you do not know? When you want to trace the history of ancient affairs, or of a lawsuit, do you not take the old records? From them you learn what the accused said, what the advocates and the defendants said, and what the judge said as he delivered his verdict. In this way you bring back to memory what had been buried in oblivion. Read, then, the records of that ancient history. When the Judge of truth took his seat, or rather, when the Physician of our failings came to the condemned man in the guise of a friend, what does he say to him? "Adam, where are you?" And what did Adam say? "I heard your voice, and I hid, because I am naked." What, then, does the One who knows all things do? He feigns ignorance and says: "And who told you that you are naked? Have you eaten from the tree from which alone I commanded you not to eat?" He shows that Adam had received an abundance of practically everything, and that it was not narrow enjoyment that led him into transgression. What, then, does the accused say to this? "The woman you gave to be with me, she gave it to me." Adam lays the sin to the woman's account, and you pin the charge on the tree? The accused could not lie at all. He found no escape outside the truth. He did not put the blame on the Creator but accused the woman. And do you accuse things whose power you do not know? And what does God say to Eve? "What is this you have done?" In answer to the question she gives the cause: "The serpent deceived me." Did she attack the creation? Did she slander the One who formed her? Did she say, "Why did you make us? Why did you forbid us the tree?" She who faced the charges found nothing to lie about. Those who are accused are fond of inventing even what does not exist, to escape the charges. Yet she, facing the charges, found no other way of escape. And do you bring forward, as an accusation against God, what the condemned themselves did not bring? But I will lead the discourse back again to our subject: "Adam, where are you?" God saw that the mouths of sinners are stopped, and that the sinner has no boldness to speak. So in the form of a question he opens to him a way to make his defense: "I transgressed and hid; but hearing your kindness, Master, I came forward to make my defense." And see the righteous Judge. He does not at once question the woman who sinned, but the man who was deceived. And rightly so. The trial would have been harsher if he had first laid hold of the guilty parties. Instead, he begins with the one who could find at least a small defense, namely that he was deceived by someone else. So he passes from the man to the woman and says: "What is this you have done?" And she says to the Master: "The serpent deceived me." The serpent deceived you? The deception would have had room to work if the commandment had not come first and shut out the error. "If I had not told you beforehand that on the day you eat from the tree you shall surely die, the deception would have had room. Why did you not follow the word of God, but accept the word of deception?" Thus the Creator was without blame, and the transgressor was liable.

But let us return to our subject. The examination of the offenses went from the man who was deceived to the woman who was deceived, but the sentence went to the one who caused the evils. Divine justice brings its verdict against him first. It is not pronounced against the man, nor at once against the woman, but against the serpent. And see how patient this justice is. God does not call the serpent to be examined, for he does not want it to shift the blame onto another or to find some other escape. What, then, does he say to it? "Cursed are you above all the wild beasts of the earth." The serpent was the visible instrument; the devil was the one who, unseen, worked the deception through the serpent. Why, then, does the punishment fall on the instrument, and why does divine justice not fall on the author of the wickedness? It proceeds both against the sin and against the instrument of the sin. You know that if a bull gores, God sets death as its penalty, though the bull has no reason. Even though it has no reason, he punishes the impulse itself. So too here he pronounces sentence against the serpent, showing that if the instrument of sin is punished like this, he will punish the one who did the work far more. This is why the blessed Isaiah, rightly taking up this threat against the serpent, says: "And it shall come to pass in the last days: God will bring his holy, great and mighty sword upon the dragon, the fleeing serpent, upon the dragon, the crooked serpent, and he will slay the dragon on that day." He calls the devil a dragon, and by the crooked serpent he means the ruler of the demons himself. So too the Savior says: "Behold, I have given you authority to tread upon serpents and scorpions." And so that you would not take him to mean visible creatures, he added: "and over all the power of the enemy."

But when you hear "dragon" and "serpent," do not think of a root of evil, as the Manichaeans say. He was not a root of evil or a nature of wickedness. He was an inclination toward lawlessness. "Do you see," they say, "how Scripture called him serpent and dragon, as if it were introducing some alien nature of wickedness?" But these words of the ungodly are empty and vain and have no reason in them. When the Lord says to human beings, "Serpents, brood of vipers," he is not condemning their nature. He is fighting against their will. So we must not be swayed by words but taught by their meanings.

But they object again and raise another question. "Why," they say, "did it call the tree 'of the knowledge of good and evil,' if the divine writing did not mean to show that the plant had some such nature?" Do not slander the truth so carelessly, man. The tree of good and evil did not produce a nature. It provided an occasion. It was given this name not because it had this by nature, but because it brought this about through the sentence passed. What did the tasting teach Adam? That it is good to obey God and evil to disobey God. That is the knowledge of good and evil, and nothing else at all. Otherwise, what knowledge of good things did he gain as soon as his eyes were opened? What other good did he see? Almsgiving? But who were the poor there? What, then, did he see? That kindness is good? But what occasion for kindness did he find? What, then, did he find? That it is good to obey one's benefactor and evil to disobey him. Who makes this clear? Scripture says: "Has it been told you, O man, what is good, or what the Lord seeks from you, but to fear the Lord your God?" Do you see that the fear of God is good, and disobeying God is evil? "The heaven shuddered," it says, "and the earth was astonished, because my people have done two evils: they have forsaken me, the fountain of living water," and so on.

"Why then," he says, "did he say, 'Do not touch the tree; if you eat of it, you will come to know good and evil through the transgression'?" Why? I will explain it to you and give you a short answer. It is always the custom of divine Scripture to give things names that match the circumstances they bring about. Here is what I mean. Isaac dug a well. The Philistines came and fought over the well and took it for themselves, reaping the fruit of another man's labor. What did Isaac do? He named the well "Enmity." The well did not cause the enmity. The quarrel over it produced the enmity, and so it became the well of enmity. He dug another well, and this too was taken from him, and he called it the well of "Injustice." This was not because the well belonged to injustice, but because the injustice found its occasion in the well. In the same way the servants of Joab and of Abner, as those who know Scripture are aware, clashed with one another at the pool and plotted against one another, and the place was called "the Portion of the Plotters." Here again the place did not produce the plotting; the event gave the place its name. So it is with Adam too. Since from what happened he was to learn by experience that obeying is good and disobeying is evil, the tree took its name from the event. But enough of this.

May we flee from that tree and run to the tree of life, the plant of the cross. It blossomed with the fruits of righteousness, put forth virginity, poured out holiness like a spring, and yielded fruits of every kind, rich with many and varied excellences. In this visible framework of wood it secured for us that greatest and most wondrous salvation: not the salvation the Savior arranged in mystery, but the one that robber openly carried off. Adam was exiled from paradise through a tree. "You are righteous, O Lord, and upright are your judgments"! For one sin Adam is exiled, and for one confession of faith the robber is brought into paradise. You are crucified with the lawless, and you save the lawless. The robber says to him: "Lord, remember me when you come in your kingdom." This robber did not stop robbing until, along with everything else, he stole the kingdom itself. But the other robber reviles the Lord: "If you are the Son of God, save yourself and us." The robber's words are kin to those of the Jews, for they too said: "If you are the Son of God, come down from the cross, and we will believe you." Do you see how the children of the devil agree in what they have learned of ungodliness? "Save yourself," he says, "and us." What does the blessed robber do? He speaks in the Lord's defense. The condemned man takes the place of a judge and begins to judge truly: "Do you not even fear God, since we are under the same sentence? And we indeed justly, for we are receiving what our deeds deserve; but what has this man done?" Tell me, robber, why did you not confess at once before Pilate? Why, after countless tortures, did you not say then what you had done? "A human judge was one thing; God as judge is another. From the first I tried to hide things, since he did not know the secrets of the heart. From this one I hide nothing, since he searches hearts." Why did you not confess at once before Pilate? "Because there punishment followed confession, but here salvation follows confession. For 'state your iniquities first, that you may be justified.'" So one could see the Savior between the robbers as a balance of justice. One could see him weighing faith against unbelief and righteousness against unrighteousness. The scale of justice swung at its center: the one, weighed down by unbelief, was dragged down, while the other, lifted up by faith, was raised high. "We indeed," he says, "are receiving what our deeds deserve; but this man, what has he done? Now I see an injustice, and a strange one: a righteous man crucified with the unrighteous, and lawfulness punished along with lawlessness. We are receiving what our deeds deserve; but what has this man done? We committed murders and made the living dead; this man made the dead alive and broke the violence of death. We plundered what belonged to others; this man urges us to give away even what is our own. We killed people who had done no wrong; this man taught us to love even our enemies. The judgment is unjust. Are his works worthy of punishment, and ours worthy of pardon? Judge truly. Let wickedness be driven out; let righteousness be honored." These things were done by the wickedness of the Jews, but the mystery revealed by the prophet was being fulfilled, which says plainly of the Savior: "And the righteous one was numbered with the lawless." So the blessed robber reasoned like a philosopher. In reproaching the other robber, he taught those who stood by. But when he saw that the ears of those present were dead, he turned at last to the one who knows the secrets of the heart and said to the Lord: "Lord, remember me in your kingdom." You see him crucified and you confess him as Lord? You see the appearance of a condemned man and you proclaim the dignity of a king? Why should we marvel, brothers, when Paul, after so much initiation into the mysteries and so much experience of miracles, says: "For if they had known, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory"? Paul proclaims this after all that initiation, after the wonders, after the signs, after countless mighty works, after the resurrection, after the ascension. But the robber, while the visible outrage was at its height and the cross stood planted, calls the crucified one Lord and says to him: "Lord, remember me when you come in your kingdom." What have you done that deserves to be remembered? What have you not done that deserves punishment? Did you not murder? Did you not steal? Did you not rob? Stained with countless evils, do you, a fountain of injustice, ask the fountain of righteousness to remember you? "Yes, Lord, you are righteous and your judgments are upright. Repay me according to your righteousness. I have seen the outrage done to you openly, and the cross, and the insults of the lawless. Yet I do not look at the visible outrage but at the hidden kingdom. I look past what I see. Will you not look past my visible offenses and accept the faith of my heart? Remember me, Lord." O just judgment! "Remember me in your kingdom. It is not just, Lord, that the devil should make one of your disciples a traitor, while you do not turn one of the devil's disciples into an evangelist. Injustice snatched away a disciple of truth; will truth not change a disciple of injustice?

For you, Master, are the one who turns darkness into light and crooked paths into straight. Turn the robber, too, into an evangelist. Conquer wickedness with goodness, quench injustice with righteousness, and give glory to your love for humankind." To it belong glory and worship to the ages of ages. Amen.
